title: Behaviors
description: Observable and covert behaviors at the situation level: what the client does, or stops doing, in response to a trigger. Fills the behavior slots of five-part, cognitive model and disorder-specific maintenance formulations. Enduring cross-situational patterns are in cs; processes such as rumination, worry, thought suppression and self-focused attention are in mp; risk levels are in rk.
sources: Thwaites-Freeston-2005 § Direct avoidance, escape and subtle avoidance
Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 2 The Core Principles of Behavioral Activation

concepts.label: Overt avoidance
concepts.definition: Not entering, or arranging life to stay away from, feared or unpleasant situations, places, people, activities or tasks.
concepts.client_wording: Staying away from places, people or tasks that make you anxious or upset.
concepts.example: Turning down a work presentation because of fear of blushing.
sources: Thwaites-Freeston-2005 § Direct avoidance, escape and subtle avoidance

concepts.label: Subtle avoidance
concepts.definition: Entering a feared situation but limiting contact with it, such as avoiding eye contact, staying at the edges or engaging only partly.
concepts.client_wording: Going along but holding back, so you never fully face what scares you.
concepts.example: Attending a party but staying in the kitchen and avoiding conversation.
sources: Thwaites-Freeston-2005 § Direct avoidance, escape and subtle avoidance

concepts.label: Escape
concepts.definition: Leaving a situation once anxiety or distress rises, which ends exposure before the feared outcome can be disconfirmed.
concepts.client_wording: Getting out of a situation as soon as the feelings get too strong.
concepts.example: Leaving the supermarket line when the heart starts racing.
sources: Thwaites-Freeston-2005 § Direct avoidance, escape and subtle avoidance

concepts.label: Avoiding bodily sensations
concepts.definition: Avoiding activities, foods or drinks that produce feared bodily sensations, such as exercise, caffeine, heat, sex or excitement.
concepts.client_wording: Steering clear of anything that makes your heart race or your body feel strange.
concepts.example: Stopping exercise because a fast heartbeat feels like the start of a heart attack.

concepts.label: Avoiding trauma reminders
concepts.definition: Avoiding people, places, conversations, objects or activities that bring back memories of a traumatic event.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping away from anything that reminds you of what happened.
concepts.example: Taking a long detour to avoid driving past the site of the crash.
sources: Ehlers-Clark-2000 § Maintaining behaviors and cognitive strategies

concepts.label: Avoidant distraction
concepts.definition: Habitually busying the mind or hands to keep feared thoughts, images, memories or feelings out of awareness.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping yourself busy or distracted so you never have to think about it or feel it.
concepts.example: Keeping music on constantly so memories of the assault cannot surface.
sources: Ehlers-Clark-2000 § Maintaining behaviors and cognitive strategies

concepts.label: Procrastination
concepts.definition: Voluntarily delaying an intended task despite expecting to be worse off, often to avoid discomfort, boredom or fear of failure.
concepts.client_wording: Putting things off even though you know waiting will make things harder.
concepts.example: Leaving the tax forms untouched until the night before the deadline.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 6 Avoidance Modification, Solving Problems, and Value-Directed Behavior

concepts.label: Escapist or numbing activities
concepts.definition: Low-effort activities such as scrolling, gaming or television, used for long periods to escape low mood or problems.
concepts.client_wording: Losing hours to your phone, games or TV to escape how you feel.
concepts.example: Scrolling social media in bed for three hours instead of replying to emails.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 6 Avoidance Modification, Solving Problems, and Value-Directed Behavior

concepts.label: In-situation safety behavior
concepts.definition: An action taken within a feared situation to prevent a feared catastrophe, which stops the person learning it would not have happened.
concepts.client_wording: Something you do to feel safe that stops you finding out you would be okay anyway.
concepts.example: Gripping a shopping cart tightly to avoid fainting.
sources: Freeman-etal-2007 § Safety behaviors in persecutory delusions

concepts.label: Carrying safety objects
concepts.definition: Keeping items believed to prevent or rescue from catastrophe, such as medication, water, a phone or a particular bag.
concepts.client_wording: Always needing certain things with you, just in case something bad happens.
concepts.example: Never leaving home without anxiety medication, even though it is rarely taken.
sources: Thwaites-Freeston-2005 § Direct avoidance, escape and subtle avoidance

concepts.label: Relying on a safe person
concepts.definition: Entering feared situations only with a trusted companion, or keeping them reachable, to feel protected from catastrophe.
concepts.client_wording: Only going places if someone you trust is with you or a phone call away.
concepts.example: Shopping only when a partner comes along.

concepts.label: Concealing signs of anxiety
concepts.definition: Efforts to hide visible anxiety, such as covering blushing, gripping objects to stop shaking or wearing dark clothes to hide sweat.
concepts.client_wording: Trying hard to hide that you are nervous so others will not notice.
concepts.example: Wearing a scarf to hide neck blushing during meetings.

concepts.label: Rehearsing and monitoring speech
concepts.definition: Mentally preparing and checking sentences before and while speaking, to avoid saying something wrong or appearing foolish.
concepts.client_wording: Practicing what to say in your head and checking every word as you talk.
concepts.example: Silently rehearsing an introduction while others are speaking.

concepts.label: Reassurance seeking
concepts.definition: Repeatedly asking others, or oneself, for confirmation that a feared outcome will not happen or that one has done nothing wrong.
concepts.client_wording: Asking again and again if things are okay, even after you have been told.
concepts.example: Asking a partner five times a day whether the door was definitely locked.
sources: Kobori-Salkovskis-2013 § Reassurance seeking in OCD and anxiety disorders

concepts.label: Checking
concepts.definition: Repeatedly verifying that something is safe, correct or done, beyond what is needed, to prevent harm or reduce doubt.
concepts.client_wording: Going back to check things over and over to make sure nothing bad happens.
concepts.example: Returning home three times to make sure the stove is off.

concepts.label: Washing or cleaning compulsions
concepts.definition: Excessive or ritualized washing, showering or cleaning, performed to remove feared contamination or to feel clean enough.
concepts.client_wording: Washing or cleaning far more than needed until it finally feels clean enough.
concepts.example: Washing hands for ten minutes after touching a door handle.

concepts.label: Ordering or arranging compulsions
concepts.definition: Arranging objects or doing actions until they feel exactly right, symmetrical or complete, to relieve discomfort or prevent harm.
concepts.client_wording: Needing things lined up or done just right, and feeling awful until they are.
concepts.example: Straightening books on a shelf until they feel exactly even.

concepts.label: Repeating or counting rituals
concepts.definition: Repeating actions, words or counts a set number of times, or until it feels right, to prevent harm or discomfort.
concepts.client_wording: Doing something again and again, or counting, until it feels safe or right.
concepts.example: Switching the light on and off six times before leaving a room.

concepts.label: Mental rituals
concepts.definition: Covert compulsions such as praying, counting, repeating phrases or mentally reviewing events, done to prevent harm or reduce doubt.
concepts.client_wording: Things you do in your head over and over to feel safe or sure.
concepts.example: Mentally replaying a conversation to check nothing offensive was said.

concepts.label: Neutralizing
concepts.definition: Voluntary attempts to cancel, undo or put right an intrusive thought or its feared consequences, overtly or in the mind.
concepts.client_wording: Trying to cancel out or undo an upsetting thought so it cannot cause harm.
concepts.example: Thinking a "safe" word after an unwanted image of harming someone.

concepts.label: Excessive acquiring
concepts.definition: Repeated buying, collecting or taking free items beyond need or space, with distress at passing them up.
concepts.client_wording: Bringing home more things than you need or have room for, and finding it hard to stop.
concepts.example: Buying extra kitchen tools on every shopping trip despite full cupboards.

concepts.label: Saving and not discarding
concepts.definition: Keeping possessions regardless of value and avoiding discarding them, leading to clutter that limits use of living spaces.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping things because getting rid of them feels too hard or wrong.
concepts.example: Keeping stacks of old newspapers that block a hallway.

concepts.label: Body-focused repetitive behavior
concepts.definition: Repetitive hair pulling, skin picking, nail biting or similar acts causing damage, often triggered by tension, boredom or perceived imperfections.
concepts.client_wording: Pulling, picking or biting at your hair, skin or nails, often without meaning to.
concepts.example: Picking at facial skin for an hour while studying.

concepts.label: Social withdrawal
concepts.definition: Reducing contact with others, declining invitations or isolating, which removes social reward and support.
concepts.client_wording: Pulling away from friends and family and spending more time alone.
concepts.example: Ignoring friends' messages and missing a weekly game night.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 2 The Core Principles of Behavioral Activation

concepts.label: Inactivity
concepts.definition: Marked reduction in routine, pleasurable or goal-directed activity, often spending long periods in bed or on the couch.
concepts.client_wording: Doing much less than before, and spending long stretches resting or lying down.
concepts.example: Staying on the couch most of the day instead of going for usual walks.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 2 The Core Principles of Behavioral Activation

concepts.label: Neglecting self-care and routines
concepts.definition: Letting basic routines lapse, such as hygiene, meals, chores, bills or medical care, which adds problems and lowers mood.
concepts.client_wording: Letting everyday things like washing, eating well or chores slide.
concepts.example: Not showering for several days and leaving dishes and mail piling up.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 5 Activity Scheduling and Structuring

concepts.label: Binge eating
concepts.definition: Eating an objectively large amount of food in a discrete period, with a sense of loss of control over eating.
concepts.client_wording: Eating a very large amount at once and feeling unable to stop.
concepts.example: Eating several packs of cookies in half an hour after a stressful call.
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 2 The Transdiagnostic View and the Cognitive Behavioral Theory

concepts.label: Dietary restriction
concepts.definition: Deliberately limiting how much, when or what is eaten, guided by strict dietary rules, to control shape or weight.
concepts.client_wording: Strictly limiting food because of rules about what, when or how much you can eat.
concepts.example: Eating nothing before 6 p.m. and avoiding all bread.
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 9 Dietary Restraint, Dietary Rules and Controlling Eating

concepts.label: Compensatory behaviors in eating disorders
concepts.definition: Acts used to undo the feared effects of eating, such as self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives or diuretics.
concepts.client_wording: Trying to get rid of food or calories after eating.
concepts.example: Purging after a binge to feel less "full of food".
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 2 The Transdiagnostic View and the Cognitive Behavioral Theory

concepts.label: Driven exercise
concepts.definition: Exercise that feels compelled, rigid or excessive, done to control shape or weight or to compensate for eating.
concepts.client_wording: Feeling you must exercise, even when ill or tired, to make up for eating.
concepts.example: Running every day despite an injury after eating dinner.

concepts.label: Eating to cope with emotions
concepts.definition: Eating, not necessarily a binge, in response to moods or events rather than hunger, to soothe or numb feelings.
concepts.client_wording: Eating to feel better when upset, bored or stressed, not because you are hungry.
concepts.example: Reaching for chocolate after every argument.
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 10 Events, Moods and Eating

concepts.label: Body checking
concepts.definition: Repeatedly scrutinizing, measuring, weighing or pinching the body to assess shape, weight or appearance.
concepts.client_wording: Checking your body over and over, in mirrors, by pinching or by weighing.
concepts.example: Pinching stomach fat and checking thigh size many times a day.
sources: Shafran-etal-2004 § Body checking and its avoidance
Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 8 Shape Concern, Shape Checking, Feeling Fat and Mindsets

concepts.label: Body avoidance
concepts.definition: Avoiding seeing, being seen or knowing about the body, such as avoiding mirrors, scales, tight clothes or photographs.
concepts.client_wording: Avoiding mirrors, scales, photos or clothes that show your body shape.
concepts.example: Refusing to be weighed and wearing only baggy clothes.
sources: Shafran-etal-2004 § Body checking and its avoidance
Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 8 Shape Concern, Shape Checking, Feeling Fat and Mindsets

concepts.label: Camouflaging appearance
concepts.definition: Hiding or disguising a perceived appearance flaw with makeup, clothing, posture or hairstyle, or by excessive grooming.
concepts.client_wording: Covering up or fixing a part of your looks you believe is flawed.
concepts.example: Wearing a cap indoors to hide perceived thinning hair.

concepts.label: Checking the body for illness
concepts.definition: Repeatedly examining the body or monitoring functions, such as pulse or lumps, for signs of serious illness.
concepts.client_wording: Checking your body again and again for signs that something is seriously wrong.
concepts.example: Pressing on a lymph node several times a day to see if it has grown.

concepts.label: Seeking medical reassurance and tests
concepts.definition: Repeatedly consulting doctors or requesting tests and scans to rule out illness, gaining only brief relief.
concepts.client_wording: Going to doctors or asking for tests over and over to be sure you are not ill.
concepts.example: Booking a third scan after two normal results.

concepts.label: Searching for health information
concepts.definition: Repeated online or other searching about symptoms and illnesses, which often raises anxiety rather than settling it.
concepts.client_wording: Looking up symptoms online again and again, then feeling more worried.
concepts.example: Spending the evening reading forums about a headache.

concepts.label: Avoiding medical care
concepts.definition: Avoiding doctors, tests, health information or illness reminders out of fear of bad news.
concepts.client_wording: Staying away from doctors or anything about illness because you fear what you might hear.
concepts.example: Ignoring a cancer screening invitation for two years.

concepts.label: Substance use to cope
concepts.definition: Using alcohol, drugs or medication beyond prescription to reduce distress, face situations or get to sleep.
concepts.client_wording: Drinking, using drugs or taking extra medication to feel calmer or forget.
concepts.example: Drinking two glasses of wine before a party to calm nerves.

concepts.label: Self-harm
concepts.definition: Intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, irrespective of apparent purpose. Code the act only, never the method, and assess risk.
concepts.client_wording: Hurting yourself on purpose, often to cope with feelings that seem too much.
concepts.example: Hurting oneself after an argument to make overwhelming feelings stop.
sources: NICE-NG225 § Terms used in this guideline: self-harm

concepts.label: Aggression
concepts.definition: Hostile acts toward people or property, such as shouting, threatening, hitting or breaking things, often driven by anger or perceived threat.
concepts.client_wording: Shouting, threatening, hitting or breaking things when angry.
concepts.example: Shouting at a partner and slamming doors after feeling criticized.
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 15 Understanding Anger, Guilt, and Shame

concepts.label: Impulsive risk-taking
concepts.definition: Acting quickly without weighing consequences, such as impulsive spending, reckless driving, unsafe sex or gambling, often under strong emotion.
concepts.client_wording: Doing risky things on the spur of the moment that you later regret.
concepts.example: Spending a month's rent online during a sleepless night.

concepts.label: Revving-up behaviors
concepts.definition: Actions that increase activation, such as taking on many projects, cutting sleep or seeking stimulation, which can escalate toward hypomania.
concepts.client_wording: Pushing yourself to go faster and do more, which can tip you into feeling too high.
concepts.example: Staying up all night starting three new business plans.

concepts.label: Appeasing or people-pleasing acts
concepts.definition: Specific acts of giving in to others against one's own wishes, such as agreeing, over-apologizing or taking on requests, to avoid disapproval.
concepts.client_wording: Saying yes, apologizing or going along with others when you really want to say no.
concepts.example: Agreeing to cover a colleague's shift despite being exhausted.

concepts.label: Self-silencing
concepts.definition: Keeping opinions, needs, feelings or limits unspoken in a situation, to avoid conflict, rejection or burdening others.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping quiet about what you think or need, so you do not upset anyone.
concepts.example: Saying nothing when a friend repeatedly cancels plans at the last minute.

concepts.label: Overworking
concepts.definition: Working excessive hours or without breaks, often driven by fear of failure or to avoid feelings, at the cost of rest and relationships.
concepts.client_wording: Working so much that rest, sleep and people you care about get squeezed out.
concepts.example: Answering work emails until 1 a.m. every night.

concepts.label: Redoing and overcorrecting work
concepts.definition: Repeatedly checking, rewriting or redoing tasks to meet perfectionistic standards, often taking far longer than needed.
concepts.client_wording: Going over your work again and again because it never feels good enough.
concepts.example: Rewriting a two-line email ten times before sending.

concepts.label: Extra time in bed
concepts.definition: Going to bed early, staying in bed late or lying awake for long periods, trying to catch up on lost sleep.
concepts.client_wording: Spending lots of extra time in bed hoping to get more sleep.
concepts.example: Going to bed at 9 p.m. after a bad night, then lying awake for hours.
sources: Edinger-etal-2021a § Recommendations: stimulus control and sleep restriction

concepts.label: Daytime napping
concepts.definition: Napping or dozing during the day or evening, which reduces sleep drive at night.
concepts.client_wording: Taking naps or dozing in the day, which can make night sleep harder.
concepts.example: Dozing on the couch for two hours in the early evening.
sources: Edinger-etal-2021a § Recommendations: stimulus control and sleep restriction

concepts.label: Irregular sleep schedule
concepts.definition: Large night-to-night variation in bedtime and rise time, including sleeping in on weekends, which disrupts the body clock.
concepts.client_wording: Going to bed and getting up at very different times from day to day.
concepts.example: Rising at 6 a.m. on weekdays and at noon on weekends.
sources: Edinger-etal-2021a § Recommendations: stimulus control and sleep restriction

concepts.label: Wakeful activities in bed
concepts.definition: Working, using screens or staying in bed while wide awake, which weakens the learned link between bed and sleep.
concepts.client_wording: Using your bed for screens, work or lying awake, so bed stops meaning sleep.
concepts.example: Answering emails on a laptop in bed until midnight.
sources: Edinger-etal-2021a § Recommendations: stimulus control and sleep restriction

concepts.label: Clock watching
concepts.definition: Repeatedly checking the time or a sleep tracker during the night, which raises arousal and worry about lost sleep.
concepts.client_wording: Checking the clock or sleep tracker during the night and counting the hours left.
concepts.example: Checking the clock every 20 minutes from 2 a.m.

concepts.label: Avoiding movement for fear of pain
concepts.definition: Avoiding or guarding physical activities and movements expected to cause pain or reinjury, which leads to disuse and disability.
concepts.client_wording: Not doing movements or activities because I'm afraid they'll hurt or harm me.
concepts.example: Stops picking up the grandchildren since the back pain started.

concepts.label: Avoiding reminders of the loss
concepts.definition: Staying away from places, objects, people, conversations and memories linked to the deceased or the death.
concepts.client_wording: Staying away from anything that reminds me of the person who died.
concepts.example: Takes a long detour so as not to pass the hospital; avoids the cemetery.
sources: Boelen-etal-2006 § Anxious and depressive avoidance strategies

concepts.label: Overdoing activity on good days
concepts.definition: Doing far more than usual when pain is lower, or persisting despite rising pain, which often triggers a flare and enforced rest.
concepts.client_wording: Overdoing it when I feel better, then paying for it.
concepts.example: Mows the whole lawn and digs the beds on a low-pain morning, then cannot move the next day.
sources: Nielson-etal-2013 § Abstract; overactivity and underactivity pacing problems
